text:
The Pump on Broad Street

In the last days of August 1854, a terrible sickness fell on Soho, a crowded district of London. Within three days of its start, more than a hundred people living near Broad Street were dead. Within ten days the toll passed five hundred. The illness was cholera, which seizes its victims with violent vomiting and diarrhoea, drains the water from the body, turns the skin blue and grey, and can kill a healthy adult in a single day.

Nobody in London knew what caused it. The accepted explanation was miasma, the belief that disease rose from foul air, from rotting waste and the stench of poor neighbourhoods. The theory seemed sensible, because cholera did strike filthy places, and the Thames in those years was little more than an open sewer. But one physician had come to doubt it.

John Snow was forty-one, the son of a Yorkshire labourer, and by then one of the most respected doctors in London. He had made his name in anaesthesia, working out careful doses of ether and chloroform, and he had given chloroform to Queen Victoria during the birth of her children. He was a quiet man who did not drink alcohol and ate plainly. He was also stubborn. During the cholera epidemic of 1848 and 1849 he had reasoned that a disease that began with stomach trouble, and not with any trouble in the lungs, must be swallowed, not breathed. He believed that something in contaminated water was passed from the sick to the healthy. He published his idea in a pamphlet, and almost no one was persuaded.

He then found a way to test it. South London was supplied by two water companies whose pipes ran down the same streets, so that neighbouring houses often drew from different sources. One company took its water from the Thames at a point downstream of the city's sewage. The other had moved its intake upriver to cleaner water. Snow and his helpers counted the deaths house by house. Homes served by the dirtier supply suffered several times as many deaths as homes served by the cleaner one, though rich and poor, young and old, were mixed on both sides. It was close to a natural experiment, and it was strong evidence. Still, it was not enough to change official minds.

When the Soho outbreak began, Snow lived only a short walk away, and he went to work at once. He suspected the water pump on Broad Street, a popular well from which hundreds of families drew their drinking water. He obtained the official list of the dead from the registrar and began visiting the houses. He asked the surviving relatives a simple question, which was where the family had got its water. Again and again the answer was the Broad Street pump. Some of those who had fled the district fell ill later, and Snow traced their steps too.

Two cases stood out. A widow in Hampstead, far from Soho, died of cholera, as did her niece. It emerged that her late husband had owned a factory in Broad Street, and that she liked the taste of the water from that pump so much that she had a bottle of it carried out to her every day. No one else in her neighbourhood fell ill. Meanwhile, there were places in Soho itself where almost no one died. The workhouse nearby, home to hundreds of poor residents, lost only a handful, because it had its own well. At the brewery on the same street the workers were left alone, because they drank their employer's beer, and the brewery too had a well of its own.

On the evening of 7 September, Snow went before the parish board of guardians, who were responsible for the neighbourhood, and laid out what he had found. He had little more than a list of names, addresses and a pattern, but the guardians agreed to act. The next day the handle was removed from the pump, so that no one could draw water from it.

Snow later drew the evidence on a map. Each death was marked by a small black bar placed at the address, and the bars clustered thickly around the pump. In an age of speculation, the picture made the case in a glance. It was not quite the first such map ever drawn, but it became among the most famous.

The epidemic was already fading by the time the handle came off, since many residents had fled and the sickest had already died, and critics later used that fact against him. The real proof came afterwards, with the help of a local curate named Henry Whitehead. Whitehead began as a sceptic, but he knew the neighbourhood and its people far better than Snow did, and he kept investigating alongside him. He found what was probably the first case, a baby girl who had died after a bout of diarrhoea in the house at 40 Broad Street just days before the outbreak. Her mother had rinsed the baby's soiled cloths and thrown the dirty water into a cesspool beneath the house. When the well was dug up, the brick lining was found to be cracked, and the cesspool was only a few feet away, leaking into the ground around it.

The authorities were slow to accept the finding. A committee reviewing the outbreak concluded that the evidence did not justify blaming the water, and the pump was soon reopened. Snow died in 1858, aged forty-five, without seeing his idea accepted. Only later, as germ science developed and the cholera bacterium was identified, was he recognised as having been right. His work is now regarded as the foundation of modern epidemiology, and it showed that disease could be tracked and stopped by counting, mapping and asking the right questions, even before anyone knew what caused it.
